analysis.one_liner: Lets other banking regulators veto consumer protection rules issued by the CFPB.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let other banking regulators overrule the CFPB with a simple majority vote, never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it much easier for other financial regulators to throw out rules written by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency that polices mortgages, credit cards, and bank fees. Under current law, the Financial Stability Oversight Council can only block a CFPB rule if two-thirds of its members agree the rule threatens the whole banking system. The bill would have lowered that to a simple majority, excluded the CFPB's own director from the vote, and allowed the Council to kill any rule it judged inconsistent with the safe operations of individual financial institutions. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and other regulated financial institutions gain the most: any CFPB rule they dislike could be blocked by a simple majority of other regulators, using a much looser standard than today. Bank trades groups had long pushed for exactly this kind of check on the bureau. Consumers could still benefit if a CFPB rule genuinely destabilized a bank, but the same mechanism applies to rules that merely cut into bank revenue from fees or lending practices.

how_it_helps.text: It would have let the Financial Stability Oversight Council — a panel dominated by banking regulators — veto any CFPB regulation with a simple majority vote, instead of the two-thirds vote the 2010 law required, and it excluded the CFPB's own director from that vote.

It lowered the standard for throwing out a CFPB rule: instead of needing to find a rule would put the whole banking system's safety at risk, the Council could set aside any rule it deemed inconsistent with the safe operations of any U.S. financial institution, and it removed the deadlines that previously forced dismissal of stale petitions.

It required the CFPB to weigh the impact of every rule on the financial safety of insured banks before issuing it, adding a bank-health consideration to a bureau whose legal mission is consumer protection.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, especially borrowers and bank customers. The CFPB's rules cover things like mortgage servicing, credit card fees, and payday lending; a system where other regulators can routinely block those rules means fewer protections and weaker enforcement for the people the bureau was created to protect.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the CFPB is a single-director agency with little accountability, and that a council of other financial regulators should be able to check rules that could weaken banks — especially smaller community banks that say consumer rules are costly to comply with.

The bill's own design lowers the bar for overturning a consumer rule from a threat to the whole banking system down to any inconsistency with an individual institution's operations, so even a well-run agency could find its work routinely blocked by the regulated industry's own regulators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered banks and other regulated companies a much easier way to kill consumer financial rules, and offered the public only the hope that safety review would catch genuinely harmful rules — a benefit the existing law already provided in emergencies. The cost was slower, weaker consumer protection on products like mortgages and credit cards, where enforcement gaps hit ordinary households hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2014, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2014 and, on the same day, was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No further action appears in the record: the committee held no markup, reported no vote, and the full Senate never considered it before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the CFPB's authority intact: under the law as it stood, the Council could block a CFPB rule only with a two-thirds vote and only if the rule threatened the whole banking system. Banks and other regulated lenders did not get the easier veto they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; banks did not get their veto

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 3, 2014; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never advanced past the Democratic-led Banking Committee, and no Democrat supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have given the banking agencies that oversee banks a standing veto over the consumer bureau's rules, with a lower bar and a simpler majority vote, and required the CFPB itself to consider bank soundness in every rule. Banks had argued CFPB regulations were costly and overreaching.

industries.industry: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (agency whose jurisdiction is at stake)
industries.note: The CFPB would have become the only financial regulator whose rules other agencies could routinely strike down, weakening its ability to police mortgages, credit cards, and bank fees on behalf of consumers.
